extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (elementary/secondary/postsecondary schools), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, and legal/compliance counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when unwelcome sex-based conduct constitutes a hostile environment under Title IX, including the enumerated multi-factor, fact-specific analysis and examples (including online conduct, sex stereotyping, and contexts across school levels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether conduct creates a hostile environment by examining the totality of the circumstances, including the nature, frequency, and context of the conduct; interpretations of Title VII inform Title IX analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the 'constellation of surrounding circumstances, expectations, and relationships' (Oncale) rather than any single factor. The factors listed are not exhaustive and the analysis must be fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hostile environment sex-based harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwelcome sex-based conduct that is subjectively and objectively offensive and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central legal standard for administrative enforcement; it need not be identical to standards for monetary damages (Davis). The terms 'subjectively and objectively offensive' and 'so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies' frame the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-exhaustive and illustrative nature of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples provided in the preamble are illustrative of contexts in which harassment may arise and do not constitute an exhaustive list of actionable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departments' examples demonstrate variety but require a 'fuller, fact-specific analysis' before reaching determinations; recipients should not rely on examples as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not based on subjective annoyance or immaturity
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal standard is not whether conduct is subjectively 'annoying' or 'immature'; instead the totality of circumstances must show unwelcome sex-based conduct that is subjectively and objectively offensive and sufficiently severe or pervasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating ordinary adolescent or annoying behavior with actionable sex-based harassment unless the full standard is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Factor — Degree of Impact (effect on access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the degree to which the conduct affected the complainant's ability to access the recipient's education program or activity (access includes the ability to participate in or benefit from the program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an individualized, fact-specific inquiry focused on the complainant; do not apply a 'perfect victim' standard or rely on assumptions about how a victim 'should' appear. Title IX Coordinator may initiate procedures considering risk of additional acts or patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on using a 'perfect victim' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must not impose notions of what a 'perfect victim' does or says or refuse to respond because a complainant is not 'traumatized enough' or is 'high-functioning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions must be individualized and cannot turn on whether a complainant exhibits particular symptoms or behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Factor — Type, Frequency, and Duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the type of conduct, frequency of incidents, and duration of conduct to inform evaluations of severity and pervasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor clarifies that multiple incidents require consideration of both how often incidents occurred and how long each incident lasted. A single social gesture (e.g., one request for a date or one gift) is generally not pervasive, but fact-specific analysis is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Factor — Ages, Roles, Previous Interactions, Other Party-specific Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate parties' ages, roles within the education program or activity, previous interactions, developmental levels, and other relevant factors about each party that may affect the impact of the conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor is relevant at all levels (including postsecondary where students may be minors or involve employees). The regulatory text was edited to remove redundant modifiers ('alleged', 'unwelcome') for consistency; consider developmental disabilities and intersection with other obligations when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Factor — Location and Context
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the location and context of the conduct (e.g., confined spaces like buses or private spaces like dorm rooms may increase intimidation; public conduct may increase humiliation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location and context inform unwelcomeness, objective/subjective offensiveness, and severity/pervasiveness. The regulation removed language about 'control the recipient has over the respondent' to avoid conflating damages-liability principles (Davis) with hostile-environment analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth Factor — Other Sex-Based Harassment in the Program
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider other sex-based harassment occurring in the recipient's education program or activity and whether multiple similar incidents (even by different respondents) create a hostile environment for the same complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This must be a fact-specific inquiry; repeated denigrating comments by multiple peers can create a hostile environment even if one isolated remark would not. A respondent's past harassment of others is not itself part of the analysis of whether current conduct created a hostile environment for the complainant, though relevant pattern evidence may be admissible in grievance procedures if related to the allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online harassment parity with in-person harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Online sex-based harassment (e.g., derogatory name-calling, nonconsensual distribution of intimate images including AI-altered/generated images, cyberstalking, sending sex-based pictures) is evaluated under the same hostile-environment factors as in-person conduct when it creates a hostile environment in the education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are not expected to affirmatively monitor students' online activity. If a school employee has information that online conduct created a hostile environment within the program/activity, the recipient must address it. The Department interprets Mahanoy and subsequent court decisions to permit schools sufficient authority to regulate certain off-campus online harassing speech in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of online examples (including AI-generated content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonconsensual distribution of intimate images (authentic or altered/generated by AI) and other digitally mediated sex-based conduct can constitute hostile-environment harassment if the totality of circumstances meets the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include consideration of technology-mediated harms when evaluating severity, pervasiveness, and effect on access/participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex stereotyping and gender identity as bases for harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Harassment based on sex stereotypes (e.g., expectations about how girls/boys should act) and harassment based on gender identity (including misgendering) can constitute sex-based harassment under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct is covered if it is sex-based, unwelcome, subjectively and objectively offensive, and sufficiently severe or pervasive. Misgendering may be harassment depending on facts; a stray or isolated remark typically will not suffice. Recipients must respect First Amendment constraints and not require violations of constitutional rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations do not require or authorize recipients to violate First Amendment rights; whether speech is regulated involves fact-specific balancing (e.g., Mahanoy and related cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should consider First Amendment doctrines in assessing discipline, recognizing that schools retain authority in many school-related and some off-campus contexts to address severe bullying or harassment targeting particular individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to elementary and secondary schools
rubrics_metrics.description: The hostile-environment definition and multi-factor test are applicable in elementary and secondary school contexts and are intended to be workable for those settings, with room for administrator judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition accounts for parties' ages and objective offensiveness, and schools long have applied fact-specific totality-of-circumstances assessments. Single severe incidents could, in some cases, suffice to create a hostile environment for enforcement purposes even if Davis limits monetary-liability claims in private suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient obligations and enforcement discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have an obligation to address sex-based harassment that creates a hostile environment; Title IX Coordinators may initiate grievance procedures even absent additional complaints based on risk, pattern, or impact on multiple individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hostile-environment elements are satisfied, recipients must act (which may include supportive measures or training) even if a particular respondent's conduct does not warrant discipline. The regulatory scheme is intended to provide adequate notice under the Spending Clause.
